utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-01-43-I, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances. For the Prosecution? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon counsel, Colonel Obrenovic. My name is Peter McCloskey. Appearing with me today is Dean Manning, the lead investigator; Mark Vlasic, a legal assistant; and Janet Stewart, the case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. For the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. My name is Zarko Nikolic. I'm an attorney at law firm Yugoslavia, and the registrar has appointed me Defence counsel for Mr. Obrenovic at his initial appearance today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And is it only for the initial appearance?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I do hear the proceedings in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And what is the date upon which you believe you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 12th of April, 1963.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And what is the address at which you resided before you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Street of Sveti Sava, 5C, Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may sit down for a moment. Mr. Nikolic, it's the common practice in the Tribunal these days for the accused to waive his right to have the indictment read out in full before entering a plea. Have you been able to discuss this with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have discussed this with Mr. Obrenovic, and he stated the following, that he received the indictment, he understood it, and there is no need for it to be read out in its entirety today. He agrees that only the counts that he has been charged with be read to him today so that he could enter his plea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does he understand that he has to plead within 30 days, but he may enter a plea today if he wishes to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Obrenovic is prepared to enter his plea with regard to the counts in the indictment today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Obrenovic, would you stand up, please, sir. In answer to Count 1 in which you are charged with complicity in genocide, do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In Count 2, you are charged with extermination as a crime against humanity. Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In Count 3, you are charged with murder as a crime against humanity. Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In Count 4, you are charged with murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war. Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And for the fifth count, you are charged with persecution on political, racial, and religious grounds as a crime against humanity. Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please. Now, Mr. McCloskey, are you able to tell me in what form the supporting material was at the time that it was presented to the confirming judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean by "form."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Was it in a redacted form or was it unredacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Unredacted, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there going to be any problem in relation to protective measures before you comply with the rather stringent requirements of Rule 66(A)(1)?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We -- in a similar trial, we had no problems, though I think that was largely because of the understanding of Defence counsel and the Prosecution that worked well together, and we don't need any -- if we can get that same understanding, we shouldn't need any special protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Then are you in a position to serve that material within the time limited?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I had a chance to speak with Mr. Nikolic today, as well as immediately before coming into court, and he would prefer not to receive anything until Colonel Obrenovic has chosen a lawyer, in which case we will be able to provide that material which we have ready to provide him when we know who is representing the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's a sensible solution. You will, of course, keep an eye on the clock, as it were. Now, may I make a suggestion so that you will be ready for it when it comes up later? Obviously a lot of the evidence in this case will be the same as it was against General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The provisions of Rule 92 bis (D), transcripts of proceedings -- transcript of evidence in other proceedings may be tendered provided it does not go to an act or the conduct of the accused. No doubt that will be taken advantage of by the Prosecution, and perhaps also by the accused. When it's going to be tendered, it would be very helpful for the Trial Chamber to have a short summary of what the Prosecution asserts is established by that evidence so -- and with references to the transcript itself. It saves an awful lot of reading, because when you do get hundreds of pages of transcript from some other trial, it's not exactly an easy task to follow, if I may say so, with respect to counsel who conduct those examinations, just what it is which is sought to be proved. So it would help the Trial Chamber very much if we have a very short statement of what the Prosecution says that transcript will prove, with a reference to the page and the lines in that transcript. It will, of course, take a little time, but it will save everybody an enormous amount of time at the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We are in a position -- as you might imagine, we have summaries for all -- most all the witnesses that will be used in this case, and it's just a matter of adapting them to the transcripts and the lines, so that shouldn't be a problem, especially when we learn what kind of length and what kind of detail you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, a little bit more than we get in those brief summaries in the pre-trial brief. It's just that having done this now in two trials where we've had long transcripts, either you spend all night reading it to keep up or you have somebody else do that exercise for you, and it seems to me very much preferable that we get somebody else to do it for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are in a position to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, is there any other matter that you wish to raise at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How about you, Mr. Nikolic? Do you want to raise any other matter at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wish to notify you of the following, that I have suggested to Mr. Obrenovic that he engage a lawyer as soon as possible to act as his Defence counsel, due to the procedure that will follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That is very important, if I may emphasise that for the sake of your client, that he does have counsel retained - that's permanent counsel - as soon as possible, because it is only in that way that the preparation for the trial can get underway. Assuming that the United Nations produces these ad litem Judges later this year, there is every chance that this case will get a hearing sometime early next year, so there should be no delays at any stage. With that, I will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
